summary: A modular monolith build: React SPA on the frontend, Go for the backend, PostgreSQL for data, hosted on Fly.io. About $1,190-4,635 a month. With 5 engineer(s), one deployable with strict internal module boundaries is the fastest and cheapest to run; modules can be extracted into services later.

frontend.justification: React SPA (Vite) is the frontend for a Realtime chat / collaboration / multiplayer project with about 10,000 daily users (~521 requests/s at peak), built by a team of 5 in 12 weeks. Search visibility is marked not needed (behind login), so rendering in the browser is acceptable, and it scores 5.0/5 for rich, app-like interaction. Next.js (React) is within 0.7 stack points, inside the tie margin (stacks this close count as tied), so either is defensible (see the runner-up note).

alternatives.why_not: Within the 1-point tie margin (counted as tied): swapped in, its stack scores 0.7 points lower; either is defensible. React SPA (Vite) is stronger on low ops burden (5.0 vs 4.0), learning curve (4.0 vs 3.0); Next.js (React) is stronger on performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0), development speed (5.0 vs 4.0); Next.js (React) takes a penalty: No search visibility needed: server rendering adds a Node.js server for pages that React SPA (Vite) serves as static files.
Ruled out: Mobile toolkit; web is a target, so the primary frontend is a web framework (mobile app suggested as companion)

backend.justification: Go (net/http, chi or Gin) serves the API at about 521 requests/s at peak (Large (5,000-50,000 users online at once)) for a team of 5. It runs as a long-running Go service, so background jobs, WebSockets and database connection pools live in one deployable process. Realtime is core, and it scores 4.0/5 on realtime fit. It leads the runner-up, Elixir + Phoenix, by 3.1 stack points (points of the overall stack score, the average of the four layer scores).

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 3.1 points. database.justification: Your data is mainly relational and reaches about 200 GB within 12 months; PostgreSQL fits relational data 5/5. You need strong consistency, and PostgreSQL gives it: a read after a write always sees that write. The workload is write-heavy, and its write scaling scores 3/5. Its share of the estimated bill is $600-$1,200 a month, against a total budget of $1,500 a month. It leads the runner-up, Microsoft SQL Server / Azure SQL Database, by 2.1 stack points.

alternatives.choice: Microsoft SQL Server / Azure SQL Database
alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 2.1 points. PostgreSQL is stronger on realtime fit (3.0 vs 2.0), portability (low lock-in) (5.0 vs 3.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 3.1 points. PostgreSQL is stronger on realtime fit (3.0 vs 2.0); MySQL takes a penalty: Customers share one database and in MySQL privileges stop at table and column level, so the tenant filter lives in every application query.

It leads the runner-up, Google Cloud Run, by 3.1 stack points.

supporting.choice: Yjs shared documents (CRDTs) synced over the WebSocket connection, with Hocuspocus or y-websocket as the sync server
supporting.justification: Many people editing one document at once need conflict-free merging; CRDTs merge concurrent edits without locks, and the server stores snapshots, not every stroke.
